beats.say: Fifteen minutes with deploy ID. That's the entire search hit on the copier glass. What starts the fifteen-minute clock?
Lift the top edge of the crop. Read the line that comes into view. A failed rollback starts the clock. Page on-call within fifteen minutes and include the deploy ID.
A chunk is a piece of a document that search can return. Copy from the condition through the ID. That one hit now gives the model a rule it can use, and a page the engineer can check.

title: What does the passage let you say?

beats.say: An engineer needs the trigger, the deadline and the ID. Try the beginning of the sentence on its own. You can quote what happened, but the passage ends at “within.” The time and the ID are both missing.

Now try the other cut. It includes the time and the deploy ID. It also runs straight into a rule about archiving notes. Which event does the fifteen-minute deadline belong to? This passage never says.

Put the original sentence back together. For this example we can run a small check. Look for “rollback failure,” “fifteen minutes,” and “deploy ID” in the candidate. All three phrases occur, and the sentence says when to page on-call.
Someone inserts two words before the action. Read the edited instruction. Predict what happens to our three matches.

All three phrases still match. An engineer following this version would do the opposite of what the source says. Use the check to catch broken cuts in these examples. Review which action, condition and exceptions the returned passage actually supports.

title: Where does a six-word window end?

beats.say: Here are the first ten words of our seventeen-word page. Count each space-separated item as one word, including “on-call.” Take the first six words. If the engineer got only that window, what unit of time could they cite?

They have the number fifteen. The word “minutes” is just across the edge. Keep the window six words wide and slide it forward four places. “Within fifteen” comes along. This time we get “within fifteen minutes with deploy ID.” Look back at what stayed behind.
The second hit has the unit and the ID, but the failed rollback sits in the first hit. Those two shared words are the overlap. Subtract two from the window size of six and you get a stride of four.

Counting from one, the first window starts at word one and the second starts at word five. In code those start offsets are zero and four. Continue by the stride until you reach the end. A real index measures its input with the embedding model's tokenizer.

title: What do the repeated words buy?

beats.say: Widen the window to seven and look at the five words in gold. Start with zero overlap. The first hit ends at “minutes.” The next has “with deploy ID.” The index stores all seventeen words once, but neither hit contains that whole gold phrase.

Repeat two words at each cut. Follow the gold marks across the second hit. One seven-word hit now contains the whole deadline and ID. We paid for that by indexing twenty-one word occurrences from the same seventeen source words.

Try four words of overlap. Now the index writes thirty-three word occurrences. The count of hits containing the gold phrase is still one. What about the entire paging rule? It stretches across ten words. Even the widest hit covers only seven.

If the question needs the governing condition, sliding a seven-word window more often won't fit that ten-word sentence. Keep the section together if it fits, or arrange to return the missing context after search.

title: What belongs with the fourteen-day window?

beats.say: Page seven already has a heading for rollback failure. The line underneath gives the paging instruction. Attach the section title to the searchable text. An engineer who finds that section can read the condition and its deadline together.

Now the same policies arrive in a table. A table row cut away from its column names still says “fourteen days” and “release summary.” Repeat the header for each row group. Now you can tell which value is the window and which is the evidence to include.
Keep the source page, version and original row span. A heading helps retrieval. The locator takes you back to the cell, where you can check qualifiers that apply to the whole table.

title: Repair a short tail under the same hard cap

beats.say: A separate training copy has a longer section. Keep its fifteen body words in order. Each smaller piece is a child of this section. A child may hold seven words, and we'd like each to have at least four. That leaves seven, seven and one.

Merge the last word into its neighbor and you get eight in the second child. Move both boundaries instead. Five, five and five fit. The character ranges below lead back to the same text. Each range includes its start and stops before its end.
Read the first five words. It has a deadline and stops before the deploy ID. Embed the heading with it and require the missing text to come back before answering.

Raise the preferred minimum to six. Two children of seven can hold only fourteen of our fifteen words, so we still need at least three. Three children of six would need eighteen words. Keep the hard cap and flag the short children for review, or use a different representation.

Return to the seventeen-word page. Stop as soon as a window reaches the end. Another copy of the tail would charge for the same words again. On a long document, twenty percent overlap advances each window by eighty percent of its width.

One divided by point eight gives about one and a quarter times as many windows. For a short page, count them directly. Our seven-word windows indexed seventeen, twenty-one or thirty-three word occurrences. None held the entire ten-word rule.

title: What counts toward the embedding limit?

beats.say: Return to the training copy. Its longer section has fifteen whitespace-separated body words and ninety-three body characters. How many tokens will the embedding model see? Run its tokenizer over the full search text, including headings and special tokens. MiniLM, the model in the article, produces a vector with three hundred and eighty-four coordinates.
Its default input limit is two hundred and fifty-six wordpieces. One number measures the output, the other limits what the model can read.

Try a smaller example with a sixteen-token input limit. Here are the tokenizer readings for this input. Twelve tokens belong to the body, three to its heading, and two are special tokens. Will the full input fit?

Add the three readings. Seventeen tokens. That puts one token beyond the limit. Split at a meaningful boundary and run the tokenizer again. It counts eleven body tokens. With the same heading and both special tokens, all sixteen fit. Check the evidence again whenever you shorten a child.
Keep the body where it is on the page. Prepend the source and section labels to the copy you embed. They use some of its token allowance. When you quote the body, follow its original span.
Record the document version and the offset units, whether characters, bytes or token positions. If ingestion normalized the text, keep the map back to the original.

Here the parser starts a new section at two Markdown heading marks. The section number belongs to our index. To locate the passage in the PDF, keep its page and original coordinates. Use a parser that understands nesting, code fences and tables when those structures occur.

For an oversized block, a recursive splitter can try paragraph breaks, line breaks, spaces, then characters. Its default counts characters. Check the final token length, and inspect any cut that separates an exception from its rule.

title: Choose the smallest chunk that can answer

beats.say: An engineer asks who to page after a rollback failure, how soon, and which ID to include. This example allows at most ten words in a single passage. Read the candidates. Which one meets the cutoff and answers the question?

The five-word fragment fits but omits the deadline and ID. The twelve-word fragment has the deadline and ID, but omits the failure condition and adds an unrelated archive rule. The ten-word rollback sentence has all three fields and meets the cutoff.
Choose the ten-word sentence. It is the shortest candidate here that answers the labeled question within the cutoff. Keep its source locator attached: incident-runbook-v3.pdf, page 7.

Let's test a cut with a question we know the answer to. This simple search counts distinct query words that occur in each passage. Count the matches down the page. The full paging sentence matches all four words.
The two fragments tie at two, and the routine rule shares only “deploy.” A tie can go to whichever fragment comes first. Neither one contains the whole instruction.

Run three small checks. For each query, look at the winning record and the phrase its text must contain. Paging, archiving and handoff each pass both checks. Those are three examples with known answers. Add exceptions, split tables and questions the runbook can't answer before comparing real systems.

Keep page seven open. Search brings back both five-word halves of the paging rule. The deadline ranks first, and the packer has ten words of evidence space. Put the deadline in first. Add the five words from the start of the sentence.
Put the selected hits in source order. Read the text the model receives. The failure condition governs the fifteen-minute deadline, and the deploy ID belongs in the page.
Change only the evidence allowance, from ten words to nine. The deadline still ranks first and uses five spaces. The packer takes whole hits. Can the second five-word hit fit?

Count the empty spaces. Only four remain. The second hit stays out. Search found the right page both times. Mark the evidence check as failed this time. When you change splitters, keep the source version and the span that supports the answer. A new cut may give that span a different chunk ID.

For a real generator, reserve room for the instructions, question and output. Suppose that leaves a hundred and twenty tokens for evidence. Two sixty-token hits fill it. Two thirty-token hits use only half.
Fill the same allowance with four of the shorter hits, then compare the answers and citations. Track repeated source spans, index size and retrieval latency alongside quality.

title: Follow a hit back to its section

beats.say: Suppose the most precise match is just “within fifteen minutes.” A short passage can make a good search target. The engineer still needs to know when to page. What words would you send along with this hit?

Use the child hit to look up its parent section. Check the parent ID, the source version and the caller's access. The pointer resolves to the permitted section on page seven. That section connects the deadline to the failed rollback.

Return one copy when two hits point to the same parent. Measure the complete packed prompt with the generator's tokenizer. The pointer helps us find the words. It takes the actual text to support the answer.

title: Can the host return this parent?

beats.say: Version four adds a sentence to the rollback section on page seven. It asks for the service name. The deadline hit and the new service-name hit both point to version four. Follow both pointers and count the parent once. All fourteen words fit in our twenty-word allowance.

Point the deadline ticket at version three. The current parent is version four, so the host rejects the stale link. Try the denied caller with both links restored to version four. The host rejects this lookup because the caller lacks access. Restore access and lower the allowance to ten words.
This time the whole parent is too long. Find a smaller complete passage or report that you lack the evidence.

Restore the twenty-word allowance. The two hits resolve to one fourteen-word section again. If other parents are needed, add the lengths of all distinct parents. Check current permissions on each child and parent, and keep the document and splitter versions with the link. Count the final prompt with the generator's tokenizer, including instructions, question and room for the answer.

title: Where does the paragraph change topic?

beats.say: If a long section has no heading at the topic change, compare neighboring sentences. For this example, count distinct words from two short lists. One list contains rollback terms, the other handoff terms. The first sentence has “rollback” and “deploy,” so its coordinates are two and zero.
The second sentence hits only “minutes.” The third hits three handoff words. We count whole words. The letters I D inside “incident” earn no point. Which pair of neighbors changes direction?
Put the first two arrows tail to tail. Both point along the rollback axis. Cosine compares directions. Divide the dot product by the product of their lengths. Two divided by two gives one.
Now keep the second arrow and lay the third at its tail. The handoff arrow makes a right angle. Their dot product and cosine are zero.
Mark a boundary when cosine is strictly below one half. One keeps the first pair together. Zero puts the cut before the commander instruction.

Try the sentence “No action is required.” It contains none of our words, so its arrow has length zero. We would be dividing by zero. Send this boundary for review. With real embeddings, tune the threshold on labeled questions. Even a clear topic change can split an exception from its condition.

Here's a different reason a search can miss. The instruction says “page the service owner.” Earlier on the same page, the runbook named Maya. If we encode only these four words, the encoder never sees her name.

Late chunking encodes a longer input first. Each token gets a vector shaped by its surroundings. Pool the vectors for the four selected words by taking their average. Now those four states have had a chance to pick up who the owner is.

Read just one coordinate from each of the four states. These are invented numbers for a Maya feature. Their mean is point seven one. Look at the four returned words. They still say “page the service owner.” To answer who, include the permitted source sentence that names Maya.

title: Which words shaped the stored vector?

beats.say: Keep the boundary around “page the service owner.” Encode the longer passage first. Use tokenizer offsets to select the four content-token states for that span and average them. Handle special tokens and normalization the way the model requires. Each selected state has already seen the shared context.
Averaging vectors that were made in separate passes can't recreate that step.

The encoder must expose token states. Its input limit and attention pattern determine how far each state can see. For longer texts, the paper encodes overlapping larger windows. The pooled method stores one vector for each child. Late interaction keeps multiple vectors for token-level scoring.

Maya's name sits in a restricted section. Everyone can read “page the service owner.” Encode those sections together and the name can shape the public vector, even if search returns only the four public words. Separate the encoder inputs by permission and trust scope.

Now only the four public words enter this pass. Store the context version with the new vector. If the caller cannot read the sentence naming the owner, this passage alone cannot support an answer about who to page.

title: What did the retrieval study measure?

beats.say: Bennani and Moslonka tested chunking on Wikipedia questions with SPLADE retrieval and a Ministral eight-billion instruction model. They varied individual chunks from fifty to five hundred tokens. They also varied how much retrieved text the generator could read, from five hundred to ten thousand tokens. Hits filled that budget in rank order.

Read the lower ruler. Sentence-preserving splits matched semantic splits up to roughly five thousand retrieved-context tokens in that experiment. The upper ruler still ends at five hundred tokens per chunk. Comparing zero with twenty percent overlap, the authors measured more indexing work without a measurable answer-quality gain in their setting.

Take a reference answer of “Maya” and a response of “MAYA” in capitals with a period. Normalizing case and punctuation gives an exact match. A semantic similarity score needs its scoring model. An abstention measure asks whether the system answered at all.
Those measures can favor different context budgets, especially when extra passages bring distractors. Check uncertainty across questions and evaluate the citations on your own runbook.

Return to the version-three records. Both have text, a source, a locator, a heading and a checksum. Look at the review decision. The complete rollback passage is ready. The deadline fragment is still under review. The manifest admits the first. That decision has to come from checking evidence for a question.
A splitter that writes “ready” on every record has never made that check.

Make a test copy of the version-three chunk. Change fifteen minutes to twenty. Hash the entire edited chunk. Its byte length stays the same, but the digits change and so does the checksum. This lets us detect the edit. Keep the ingestion checksum for the source document separately.
Record the immutable version, span and splitter configuration so a new ingestion can replace the old records. Establish the producer's identity and the accuracy of the rule separately.

For this runbook, start with one section per heading when it fits. Keep table headers and provenance. Split oversized sections, then check the full embedding input. Carry trust and authorization scope with the record.
Quarantine excludes a source, and permission still applies when a child expands to a parent. Test extra overlap or a different encoder against the specific question that failed.

Read page seven of version five. The deadline has changed. Use the wording on this page to decide what belongs in the message. You have eighteen words of evidence space. Search ranks the last nine words first. The first nine words rank second. Both hits are permitted.
Read the two nine-word strips in source order. When should the engineer page, and what goes in the page?

After a rollback failure, page on-call within twenty minutes. Include the deploy ID and identify the service. The page leaves the form of that service identifier open. Now lower the allowance to twelve words. The first-ranked hit takes nine. Three spaces remain for another nine-word hit. The condition was in the skipped hit.

Replay the eighteen-word request. It admitted both hits. Lay the two hits over the original page. Count the cells between the two bands. From on-call through deploy, six words occupy the same positions. That request paid for eighteen word occurrences across twelve distinct positions. It charged those six shared words twice.

Return to the twelve-word request. Only the first hit fit. Follow the first hit to its current, permitted parent. Replace the hit with one copy of the section. All twelve words fit. The condition is back beside the deadline.

One last ticket. Same permitted parent and same question. Slide the stop back to eleven words. This host returns parents whole. This is the only approved complete passage for the question. Answer or abstain?

Abstain. The parent extends one word past the stop. Add one word of capacity. The whole rule fits. Now answer and cite page seven of version five. Test both requests when you change your splitter. In the next lesson we'll ask what an evaluation score actually establishes.
